thread.title: Vermont Agency of Education releases Read Vermont report amid funding uncertainty
thread.title_full: Vermont Agency of Education releases Read Vermont report amid funding uncertainty

author: M. A. Tomlin
title: Vermont Agency of Education releases Read Vermont report amid funding uncertainty
text:
Zoie Saunders, Secretary | Vermont Agency of Education
The Vermont Agency of Education released its first-year implementation report on Read Vermont as the program faces an uncertain future in the General Assembly, according to a May 6 statement.
Read Vermont is the state's main literacy initiative, launched in 2024 to improve literacy instruction through training based on the science of reading. The program follows strategies credited with improving literacy rates nationwide but may need to be scaled back after lawmakers did not include funding for it in their initial draft of the fiscal year 2027 budget.
"The Governor's request to fund Read Vermont represents Vermont's first targeted state investment in literacy since the passage of Act 139 of 2024," said Secretary of Education Zoie Saunders. "This investment, which does not require new spending, is an important first step in regaining Vermont's national leadership in literacy. A budget is an expression of priorities, and I look forward to working with the legislature to prioritize supporting educators in teaching every child in Vermont how to read."
Read Vermont has served as the agency’s coordinated strategy for implementing Act 139 of 2024, a law that aimed to change how teachers deliver literacy instruction but did not provide dedicated funding for implementation. The agency initially used federal funds to start Read Vermont; however, these funds are running out due to changing priorities and will end at this fiscal year's close. In January, Governor Phil Scott requested $700,000 be reallocated for Read Vermont so that existing funds could be used without seeking new money. Despite advocacy from both the agency and administration throughout this legislative session, lawmakers have yet to allocate funding for Read Vermont. Both chambers recently passed a $9.4 billion FY27 budget that does not include money for literacy initiatives; final decisions will be made later this month.
Recent data show ongoing challenges: only 31% of fourth graders and 29% of eighth graders achieved reading proficiency on the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) in 2024. Among economically disadvantaged students those numbers were even lower—18% and 17%, respectively—with overall results placing Vermont below national averages for the first time.
“Evidence from the science of reading research continues to emphasize the importance of systematic, explicit and strategic instructional practices in phonological awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension,” said Lori Dolezal, Curriculum and Instruction Director at the Agency of Education. “Read Vermont is our ongoing, comprehensive, data-driven approach to improving teaching, learning, and student outcomes using theories and practices from science-of-reading literature.”
The report highlights early progress since its launch: hundreds of educators statewide have participated in professional learning sessions; more than thirty staff members received training; universal screening has become common practice—92% use early reading screeners recommended or approved by the agency—and screening data reveal that while about one-third met proficiency benchmarks another third performed below them.
To continue advancing its goals if funded further steps are planned including strengthening universal screening requirements partnering with certification boards issuing criteria for instructional materials by summer next year expanding coaching opportunities contingent upon resources being available.
While initial progress has been achieved using limited resources sustaining these efforts will require continued state commitment beyond current requests as scaling up would demand greater investment similar those seen during historic improvements elsewhere.
